sentences.text: A kestrel hunting hangs in the air.

That is the thing about them that everybody notices first and that Tomás's father had explained to him when he was about six, on the way to somewhere, in the way of a man filling four minutes in a car.
She faces the wind and she flies forward at exactly the speed the wind is coming at her, and the two cancel, and she stops.
Not gliding, not soaring — actively flying, hard, and staying in one place.
Her head does not move at all.
The body shifts and the wings work and the tail spreads and closes, and the head hangs there in the air as though it has been nailed to a point in the sky.
Then she moves a dozen metres and does it again over the next patch.
That is the whole method.
She holds still, she looks, she moves on.
A field is searched in about forty minutes.

The reason she has to hang there, his father had said, is that she is looking for something that is trying not to be seen, in grass, from twelve metres up, and the only way to do that is to hold your eye absolutely still over one patch until the patch gives something away.
Everything about the bird is built round that one requirement.
The wings are doing enormous work.
The tail is doing continuous small corrections.
The head is doing nothing at all, and the doing-nothing is the entire point of the rest of it.
Tomás had thought that was the best thing he had ever heard and had told several people at school, who had not agreed.
Which is why, when she stopped moving on, Tomás noticed.

He was thirteen and he went past the Vasco field twice a day on the bike, and on the Monday she was hanging over the near corner, and on the Tuesday she was hanging over the near corner, and on the Wednesday morning she was over the near corner and he stopped the bike and put his foot down and watched her for twelve minutes.
She was working.
That was what was wrong.
She was not perched somewhere with a good view, saving her energy, which is what a bird does when it is not hunting.
She was hovering — which is expensive, which is the most expensive thing a small bird can do — over one patch of ground about the size of a garage, for a third day.
There was nothing there.
He could see the whole of it from the road.
Stubble, a bit of thistle, the concrete pad where a shed had been.
